cards.title: Grief can follow many kinds of loss, not only a death
cards.body:
Grief is the natural response to losing someone or something that mattered to you. The NHS points out that it is not only death that brings it on. The end of a relationship, losing a job, moving away from home, or watching someone you love become seriously ill can all bring real grief.

Naming it as grief can help. It explains why you may feel low or exhausted after a change other people see as minor, and it gives you permission to look after yourself instead of telling yourself to just get on with it.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent change in your life that still weighs on you. Could part of what you feel be grief? Write one sentence naming what you lost.

quiz.question: According to the NHS, which of these can cause grief?
options: Only the death of a close family member
Only sudden or violent deaths
Losses such as a break-up, losing a job or moving home
Only losses that happen in childhood
quiz.explanation: The NHS lists many causes of grief, including the end of a relationship, job loss, moving home and a loved one's serious illness.

cards.title: Shock and numbness are a common first reaction to loss
cards.body:
In the first days after a loss, many people do not feel what they expect to feel. The NHS describes shock and numbness as common early reactions: you may feel dazed, distant, or strangely calm, as if it has not really happened.

This is not a sign that you did not care. It is one of the ways a mind copes with news too big to take in at once. Other feelings, such as deep sadness, crying and tiredness, often arrive later, sometimes in waves.
cards.apply_it: If someone you know seems oddly calm after a loss, resist judging it. Offer quiet, practical help instead, such as a meal or a lift.

quiz.question: What does feeling numb soon after a death usually mean?
options: The person did not love the one who died
It is a common early reaction to a loss that is hard to take in
The grief is already over
The person needs to be told to cry
quiz.explanation: The NHS lists shock and numbness among the common first symptoms of grief.

cards.title: Anger and guilt are normal parts of grief, too
cards.body:
Grief is not only sadness. The NHS notes that many bereaved people feel angry, at the person who died, at the circumstances, at doctors or at life itself. Many also feel guilty: about things they said or never said, or a belief that they should have been able to stop the death.

These feelings can be confusing and even shameful to admit. Knowing they are a common part of grief can ease the extra burden of thinking something is wrong with you. Talking them through with someone you trust often makes them easier to carry.
cards.apply_it: If you feel guilt about a loss, write down what you wish you had said. Then write what a kind friend would say back to you.

quiz.question: Which feelings does the NHS describe as common in grief, besides sadness?
options: Anger and guilt
Only relief
Only boredom
Nothing: grief is sadness alone
quiz.explanation: Anger at the person or the circumstances, and guilt about things said or unsaid, are listed as common symptoms.

cards.title: Grief doesn't always look like grief
cards.body:
The NHS points out that grief is not always obvious. Its feelings can come and go, and strong emotions can surface without warning, weeks or months later. Because of this, it can be hard to connect a change in someone's behaviour, such as irritability, withdrawal or exhaustion, with a loss.

This is worth remembering for yourself and for others. A colleague who has become short-tempered, or a relative who no longer joins in, may be grieving. Gentle curiosity is kinder than assuming they are simply being difficult.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose mood has changed lately. Has there been a loss in their life? Consider checking in with a simple 'How are you really doing?'

quiz.question: Why can grief be hard to recognise?
options: It always passes within a week
It only affects children
Its feelings can come and go and surface without warning, so changes are not always linked to the loss
It never affects behaviour
quiz.explanation: The NHS notes grief doesn't always look obvious and can be hard to link to changes in behaviour.

cards.title: The stages of grief are not a fixed path
cards.body:
The NHS describes stages that many people recognise: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. It is careful to add that people do not necessarily go through all of them, or in any set order.

It also clarifies what acceptance means: coming to terms with the loss, not liking it or feeling fine about it. So if you move back and forth between feelings, skip some, or never feel 'done', you are not grieving wrongly. The NHS adds that for most people grief becomes less intense over time.
cards.apply_it: If you have ever felt you were 'behind' in grief, remind yourself today: there is no correct order and no deadline.

quiz.question: What does the NHS say about the stages of grief?
options: Everyone goes through all five in order
Acceptance means you are happy about the loss
Skipping a stage means grief went wrong
People may not go through all of them, or in a set order
quiz.explanation: Stages are common, but not everyone experiences all of them or follows a fixed order. Acceptance means coming to terms with the loss.

cards.title: Talking to someone you trust lightens the load
cards.body:
One of the first things the NHS suggests is talking: to a friend or family member you trust, a health professional, or a counsellor. Peer support, where you meet others who have lived through a similar loss, is another option many people find helpful.

Talking does not remove the loss, but it can stop you carrying it alone. Different people help in different ways: one friend may be good at listening, another at practical help. In many communities, faith leaders and elders also offer this support.
cards.apply_it: Name one person you could talk to honestly about a loss. Send them a short message today, even just 'Can we talk this week?'

quiz.question: Which of these does the NHS suggest when coping with grief?
options: Keep your feelings to yourself
Talk to someone you trust, a professional or a peer support group
Only talk once you feel better
Avoid anyone who knew the person
quiz.explanation: Talking to people you trust, health professionals, counsellors or peer support groups can help.

cards.title: Look after your body while you grieve
cards.body:
Grief is tiring, and it is easy to stop eating properly or moving at all. The NHS suggests two simple things that can help: regular, healthy meals and regular exercise.

These are not cures for sadness. They are ways of keeping your body steady enough to carry what you are feeling. A walk around the block, a plain meal at the usual time, or a glass of water count. When friends ask how they can help, food and company on a walk are good answers.
cards.apply_it: Today, eat one proper meal at a regular time and take a short walk, even ten minutes.

quiz.question: What physical habits does the NHS suggest during grief?
options: Regular healthy meals and regular exercise
Fasting until the feelings pass
Staying in bed as much as possible
Training hard to forget the loss
quiz.explanation: The NHS suggests eating regular, healthy meals and exercising regularly.

cards.title: Set small goals instead of trying to do everything at once
cards.body:
After a loss there can be a flood of things to deal with, alongside the feelings themselves. The NHS advises against trying to do everything at once. Setting small, achievable goals is more realistic.

One phone call, one form, one cupboard. Each small task completed is real progress, and it leaves energy for rest. The NHS also suggests not dwelling on things you cannot change; your attention is precious and better spent on the next small step.
cards.apply_it: Write down everything you feel you must do, then circle just one small task to finish today.

quiz.question: What does the NHS recommend about tasks after a loss?
options: Finish everything in the first week
Avoid all tasks for months
Let other people decide everything
Set small, achievable goals rather than doing everything at once
quiz.explanation: Trying to do everything at once can overwhelm you; small achievable goals help.

cards.title: Alcohol, drugs and gambling make grief harder, not easier
cards.body:
When feelings are overwhelming, it is tempting to numb them. The NHS specifically advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with grief.

These can feel like relief in the moment, but they tend to deepen low mood, disturb sleep and create new problems on top of the loss. If you notice yourself reaching for them more often, that is a sign to talk to someone, such as a GP, a counsellor or a support service, rather than a reason for shame.
cards.apply_it: Notice what you reach for when grief hits hardest. Choose one gentler alternative for next time, such as calling a friend or going outside.

quiz.question: What does the NHS advise about alcohol and gambling during grief?
options: They are a safe way to relax
Use them only at weekends
Don't use them to cope
They help you sleep better
quiz.explanation: The NHS lists alcohol, cigarettes, gambling and drugs as things not to use to cope with grief.

cards.title: You are not as alone as grief makes you feel
cards.body:
Grief can feel isolating, as if no one else could understand. The NHS lists believing you are alone as one of the things to avoid, and points to support from friends, family, health professionals and bereavement charities.

In the UK, for example, Cruse Bereavement Support helps adults, and other organisations support families after the death of a baby or child, or a loss by suicide. Many countries have similar services, and religious and community groups often offer support too.
cards.apply_it: Search for one bereavement service, helpline or support group in your area and save its contact details, for yourself or someone else.

quiz.question: Which belief does the NHS suggest letting go of when grieving?
options: That support exists
That you are completely alone with it
That grief changes over time
That talking can help
quiz.explanation: The NHS advises against believing you are alone; support is available from people and organisations.

cards.title: Know when to ask a doctor for help
cards.body:
Sadness after a bereavement usually eases gradually. The NHS suggests seeing a GP if you are struggling to cope with stress, anxiety or low mood, if low mood has lasted more than two weeks, or if the things you are trying yourself are not helping.

In England, adults can also refer themselves to NHS talking therapies without seeing a GP first. Wherever you live, a doctor or local health service can point you to support. If you are in crisis or thinking of harming yourself, get urgent help straight away.
cards.apply_it: Check where you would go for help in your area if low mood after a loss lasted more than two weeks. Note the number somewhere easy to find.

quiz.question: When does the NHS suggest seeing a GP after a bereavement?
options: Only if you stop crying
Never: grief should be handled alone
Only after a year has passed
If low mood lasts more than two weeks or self-help isn't working
quiz.explanation: The NHS suggests seeing a GP if you can't cope, low mood lasts over two weeks, or your own efforts aren't helping.

cards.title: For some, grief stays very intense: that deserves support
cards.body:
For most people grief softens over time, but the NHS describes prolonged grief disorder, where grief stays very intense for many months or years. Signs can include sadness or guilt that does not change, constant thoughts about the person who died, finding it very hard to accept the death, and being unable to return to daily life.

It is more likely after a sudden, unexpected or traumatic death. This is not a weakness. If it sounds familiar, the NHS advises speaking to a GP, and anyone having suicidal thoughts should seek help urgently.
cards.apply_it: If grief has stayed unchanged and overwhelming for a long time, book an appointment with a doctor this week and take a note of what you've been feeling.

quiz.question: According to the NHS, prolonged grief disorder is more likely after which kind of death?
options: A sudden, unexpected or traumatic death
A death expected for many years
The death of a pet
Any death in old age
quiz.explanation: The NHS says it is more likely if the death was sudden, unexpected or traumatic.

cards.title: Be honest with children about a death, and include them
cards.body:
When a child loses someone, adults often want to protect them from the truth. The NHS recommends direct, honest communication instead, and talking about the person who has died, whether a grandparent, parent, sibling or friend.

Leaving a child out of family ceremonies can make them feel shut out. The NHS suggests talking as a family about how the child can take part in events to remember or say goodbye, in ways that fit your family's traditions. Photos, stories and games can help children share their feelings.
cards.apply_it: If a child in your life has lost someone, invite them to share a favourite memory or story about that person.

quiz.question: What does the NHS recommend when a child is bereaved?
options: Avoid mentioning the person who died
Keep the child away from all ceremonies
Talk honestly and involve the child in remembering
Wait until they are adults to explain
quiz.explanation: Direct, honest talk and including children in remembering helps; excluding them can make them feel left out.

cards.title: Children grieve in their own way and time, often through play
cards.body:
The NHS notes that children may bring up their loss at different times and in different ways, sometimes long after the event. Young children might talk about death or act it out in play. This is normal: it is how they make sense of what happened.

A memory box can help. Together with the child, you can fill it with gifts, photos, written memories or objects such as shells from a day out, anything that helps them feel connected to the person who died.
cards.apply_it: Gather three small objects or photos that remind a grieving child of the person they lost, and offer to start a memory box with them.

quiz.question: What does it usually mean when a young child acts out death in play?
options: They are being disrespectful
They are trying to make sense of what happened
They have forgotten the person
They need to be stopped at once
quiz.explanation: The NHS describes talking about death or acting it out in play as a normal way for children to understand a loss.

cards.title: Support children before a death, and look after yourself too
cards.body:
The NHS notes that a child's stress is often highest before someone dies, because of fear and uncertainty. Pre-bereavement counselling can give them space to talk about their worries. A parent who knows they are dying might make a memory box with or for their child, as a lasting link.

The page also reminds parents and carers that they need support after a loss too. Getting help for your own grief is not selfish: it makes it easier to support the children who depend on you.
cards.apply_it: If you are supporting a grieving child, name one person or service who can support you as well, and reach out to them.

quiz.question: When does the NHS say a child's stress around a death is often highest?
options: Before the death, because of fear and uncertainty
Only years later
On the day of the funeral only
Children don't feel stress about death
quiz.explanation: A child's stress is often at its highest before a death, which is why pre-bereavement support can help.

cards.title: After a baby dies, parents can choose how to make memories
cards.body:
The death of a baby is devastating, and the NHS stresses that there is no right or wrong way to respond. After a stillbirth, parents can choose whether to see and hold their baby, give them a name, take photos, or keep mementoes such as a lock of hair, hand or footprints, or a blanket.

If they are unsure, hospitals can often store keepsakes for later. Guilt, anxiety and depression are common afterwards, for both parents. Talking to a GP, midwife or other bereaved parents can help, and charities such as Sands offer helplines.
cards.apply_it: If someone you know has lost a baby, use the baby's name if they have given one, and simply say you are sorry.

quiz.question: What does the NHS say about the choices parents make after a stillbirth?
options: Parents must hold their baby
Photos are not allowed
Keepsakes must be decided on immediately
They are personal decisions with no right or wrong answer
quiz.explanation: Seeing, holding, naming and keeping mementoes are all personal choices; hospitals can store keepsakes if parents are unsure.

cards.title: After a miscarriage, both partners may need support
cards.body:
The NHS notes that after a miscarriage you may feel many emotions, including anxiety and deep upset, and that coming to terms with it emotionally can take longer than physical recovery.

Support is available for partners too, who may grieve quietly while focusing on the person who was pregnant. Talking with each other, family or friends helps. You may be offered counselling or can ask for it, and support groups, in person or online, connect you with others who understand.
cards.apply_it: If you or your partner have been through a miscarriage, ask each other one gentle question: 'How are you really feeling about it?'

quiz.question: What does the NHS say about support after a miscarriage?
options: Only the pregnant person needs support
Support is available for partners too, and counselling can be asked for
Emotional recovery is always quicker than physical
Talking about it makes things worse
quiz.explanation: Partners can be affected as well; counselling and support groups are available.

cards.title: When someone you love is dying, everyone is grieving at once
cards.body:
The NHS page on coping with a terminal illness reminds us that loved ones are also working through their own feelings about the diagnosis. That can make conversations hard on both sides, and a counsellor or someone less close can help.

It suggests taking things a day or a week at a time, writing worries down, and accepting offers of help. Being specific works best: say if you need shopping done, meals for the freezer or lifts to appointments. Groups such as Samaritans are there for difficult nights.
cards.apply_it: If someone close to you is seriously ill, offer one specific, concrete form of help this week rather than 'let me know if you need anything'.

quiz.question: What does the NHS suggest when accepting help during terminal illness?
options: Refuse help to stay independent
Wait for people to guess what you need
Be specific about what you need, such as meals or lifts
Only accept help from professionals
quiz.explanation: Accept offers of help and be specific, such as shopping, meals or lifts to appointments.
